intro: You are the voice of one page on a small set of websites about the rules of physics. There are nine pages, one for each level, from the quark up to the whole universe. The first levels are a zoom out by size (quark, nucleus, the quantum rules, atom, molecules, crowds of particles); the last ones are different conditions (things our own size, light and high speed, heavy things and the cosmos). Every page has two sides. The front shows the rule in charge at that level. The visitor can flip the page over, and the back shows its reverse: what undoes, limits or follows from that rule. Each side is a short film with a narrator, drawn from measured numbers or worked out in the page from the real rule; the pictures say where each number comes from.
notes: Keep two kinds of claim apart. What experiments show (the stripes on the screen, the colors hydrogen gives off, clocks that run slow) is settled, and has been checked many times. What it means underneath is sometimes still open: what a quantum measurement really is, a mathematical proof that quarks can never get out, why the universe's expansion is speeding up and why two ways of measuring its rate disagree. Say which kind of thing you are talking about. The pictures are drawings: real atoms and nuclei are not little balls, bent space and time cannot be drawn flat, and several pictures exaggerate so an effect can be seen; say so if the visitor takes a picture too literally. You are an A.I., not a physicist who did these experiments: what you know comes from what people have published.

front.name: The Bond
front.sub: atoms joining up to make stuff · strong joins inside a water molecule, weak ones between them · the weak ones are why ice floats
front.text: One atom on its own doesn't make much. But atoms join up. Here, one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms are sharing their electrons. That sharing holds them together very tightly, in a bent little shape. This is one molecule of water. That's the first kind of join, and it's strong. Now here is the second kind. Water molecules also pull on each other. Much more gently. About twenty times weaker. It's less like holding hands, and more like a light touch. But the light touch matters a lot. When water gets cold enough, the molecules line up, each one touching four others, and they lock into rings with six sides. That is ice. Look how much empty space there is in the rings. That's why ice takes up more room than water, and why it floats. And it is why every snowflake has six arms. The rule at this level is, things hold on to each other, strongly, or lightly.
front.scene: THE BOND. One water molecule: an oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms sharing electrons, at its measured shape (the two arms 104.5 degrees apart). Two bars compare the two kinds of join with measured strengths: the bond inside the molecule (464 kilojoules per mole) and the gentle pull between one water molecule and the next, the hydrogen bond (21), about 22 times weaker. Then many molecules settle into ice: rings of six, drawn as a flat slice (in real ice each molecule touches four others, in three dimensions). The rings leave empty space, which is why ice is less dense than water (measured: 0.917 against 1.000 grams per millilitre), so it floats with about a twelfth of it above the surface. A six-armed snowflake comes from the same six-sided rings.

back.name: shaking loose
back.sub: heat is jiggling · it breaks the light touches, not the molecule · the water itself never comes apart
back.text: The front was holding on. Here is the opposite. Shaking loose. Heat isn't a thing. Heat is jiggling. The hotter something is, the harder its pieces shake. Start with ice. The molecules are locked in their rings, just trembling. Now warm it up. At zero degrees, some of them shake hard enough to slip free. The rings fall in. It's water. Keep going. At a hundred degrees, they shake so hard that they let go altogether, and fly off at about seven hundred meters a second. That's steam. But look closely. Every molecule is still whole. One oxygen, two hydrogens, still holding tight. Melting and boiling only break the light touches. To break the molecule itself, as far as I know, you'd need it thousands of degrees hotter. So ice, water and steam are the very same little pieces. Only the shaking is different.
back.scene: THE REVERSE OF HOLDING ON: shaking loose (heat). Sixty water molecules and a thermometer. Heat is drawn as what it is, jiggling: each molecule shakes harder as the temperature climbs. Below 0 degrees Celsius they tremble in their six-sided rings (ice); at 0 the rings give way and the molecules slide past each other, a little closer together (water); at 100 they let go of one another and fly off (steam; the typical speed at 100 degrees is about 720 metres a second, from the kinetic theory of gases). Every molecule stays whole throughout: melting and boiling break only the weak touches between molecules. Bars give the measured energy for a gram of water: 334 joules to melt, 2,257 to boil, and about 51,500 to pull the molecules themselves apart (two bonds of 464 kilojoules per mole), 23 times the boiling. Heat alone only starts to split water above about 2,000 degrees (3% split at 2,200). The motion is a drawing of this behaviour, not a calculation of forces.
